name: Michigan

notes: Food for home consumption is exempt, candy and soft drinks included; prepared food is taxed.
Alcohol bought in stores: beer, wine and liquor are taxed at 6%, served or bought to take home; spirits also carry three 4% specific taxes built into the state's minimum shelf price.

Cigarettes and other tobacco are taxed at 6%, on top of their excise taxes; vapor products and nicotine pouches carry no state excise (none enacted as of October 2026; the governor proposed one in her 2027 budget, as reported).
Personal care products: menstrual products have been exempt since February 3, 2022, which is not taken out here; diapers are taxed.
Barber and beauty services, and laundry and dry cleaning: not taxed (FTA 2017 survey answer).
Motor fuel has been exempt from sales and use tax since January 1, 2026 (Public Acts 17 and 19 of 2025), replaced by a higher per-gallon fuel tax (52.4 cents for 2026, indexed to inflation).
Repair labor is not taxed when it is itemized separately from parts.
Michigan has no local sales taxes, and state law (2017 Public Act 135) bars local taxes on food and drink.

Hotel rooms carry the 6% use tax, a convention facility tax of 1.5% to 6% at larger hotels, and county accommodations taxes and tourism assessments of up to 5% (8% with a vote), which this site does not count.
gaps: Michigan has no local general sales tax; the 6% state rate applies everywhere. A local sales tax (proposed for Detroit) would need a constitutional amendment, a state law and a local vote (Citizens Research Council, January 2026).

programs: Michigan's Renaissance Zones aren't shown: the area-wide zones have all expired, and those still running are single company sites (Michigan Strategic Fund, 2023 report). Neighborhood Enterprise Zones, which abate taxes on homes, aren't shown either.

Tax increment authorities are mapped for Detroit, Oakland County's cities and townships, Grand Rapids, Mason and Kalamazoo (its downtown development authority, Downtown Economic Growth Authority and Northside Cultural Business District Authority); business improvement districts for downtown Detroit and Grand Rapids. Not mapped: Ann Arbor's downtown development authority (it grew in April 2026, and the City's map couldn't yet be confirmed to include the addition), Lansing's, Flint's and Traverse City's authorities and Lansing's principal shopping district (no map from the city found), Detroit's new Rivertown business improvement zone (approved by owners; only its organizers' map was found), Grand Rapids' Monroe North tax increment authority (status unconfirmed) and Detroit's transformational brownfield plans, which are site by site.

warn.text: Traverse City draws many visitors, but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy: its seasonal homes (6.8%) and its 28 lodging places (1.7 per 1,000 residents) fall under the flag's cutoffs, though 2 of its 4 census tracts are flagged on their own. Visitors' spending is part of Traverse City's local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.
